content.heading: 💡 2-4 Young's Experiment
content.html: Young was a British scientist who lived from 1773 to 1829, and he was the first to carry out an experiment on the superposition of two light waves. To illustrate the basic idea and recreate what Young did, we need to set up the following: a piece of aluminum sheet and a piece of copper wire. We pull the copper wire until it breaks, and make two small holes close to each other in the aluminum sheet. We then hold the sheet up in front of one eye and observe a small lamp some distance away. To carry out the experiment and take measurements, we use the setup shown in Figure 2-3.

content.heading: 🕹️ Recreating Figure 2-3: The Apparatus Setup of Young's Experiment

content.html:
The interference pattern contains regular bright and dark lines from the two slits; these lines are called Young's fringes. From the figure shown, starting from right to left, we can estimate that the interference pattern covers 1 cm of the screen.

Constructive interference — the bright line — occurs when the path difference equals a whole number of wavelengths. If (a) is small compared to the slit separation and (D) is the screen's distance from the slits, with \((D>a)\), then \((S_1P\) and \(S_2P)\) are nearly parallel, and the wavelength is (λ).

content.heading: 📋 Meaning of the Symbols in the Relation
items: \(X\) — the distance between a fringe and the central fringe, measured in meters (m).
\(a\) — the separation between the two slits, measured in meters (m).
\(D\) — the distance between the slits and the screen, measured in meters (m).

content.html: If the eyepiece is moved by an amount \(\Delta X\) from one maximum, say \(n=3\), to the next maximum, say \(n=4\), it moves a distance of \(\Delta X\), which is called the fringe spacing.

content.svgAriaLabel: Young's fringe pattern on the screen
content.descriptionHtml: Choose the light's color (its wavelength), move the sliders for the slit separation (a) and the screen distance (D), and watch the pattern of bright and dark fringes change live on the screen, with the fringe spacing \(\Delta X\) computed live.

ruleBoxes.html: Fringe spacing \( \Delta X = \dfrac{\lambda D}{a} = \) 0.85 mm

content.problemHtml: In Young's experiment using a sodium lamp with a wavelength of (590 nm), placed (0.96 m) from the screen, the distance between the fourth fringe and the central fringe was (3.2 mm). Calculate the separation between the slits.
content.label: 📝 Example (1)

given: \( \lambda = 590\ \text{nm} = 590\times10^{-9}\ \text{m} \) — wavelength of the sodium light (after conversion)
\( D = 0.96\ \text{m} \) — distance between the slits and the screen
\( X = 3.2\ \text{mm} = 3.2\times10^{-3}\ \text{m} \) — distance between the fourth fringe and the central fringe (after conversion)
solution.required: Calculate the separation between the slits \(a\).

steps.note: We rearrange the relation \(\lambda=aX/nD\) to find \(a\)

content.heading: 📋 Young's Experiment Is Used For
items: Studying the phenomenon of constructive interference in light.
Determining the wavelength of monochromatic light.
Determining the distance between two successive fringes of the same type.
Investigating the nature of light and proving its wave nature.
Proving the existence of the wave property in all particles, such as electrons and others.

content.html: The pattern of constructive-destructive fringes depends on the optical path difference between the two reflected waves. If the optical path difference equals a whole number of wavelengths \((\lambda)\), it represents constructive interference; but if the optical path difference \((S_1,S_2)\) equals an odd number of half-wavelengths \(\left(\tfrac12\lambda\right)\), the interference is destructive, as mentioned earlier.

$$ \delta = a\sin\theta $$

The optical path difference \(\delta\) between the two rays emerging from the slits at an angle θ from the central axis (Figure 2-5).
It is impossible to obtain interference fringes in Young's experiment when the separation between the slits is less than the wavelength of the incident light.

questions.question: The regular bright and dark lines produced by Young's experiment are called:
questions.explain: These regular bright and dark lines are called Young's fringes.

questions.question: In the relation \(\lambda=aX/nD\), the symbol (D) represents:
options: the distance between the slits and the screen
questions.explain: (D) represents the distance between the slits and the screen, measured in meters.

questions.question: If the separation between the slits (a) increases while the other variables stay constant, the fringe spacing \(\Delta X\):
questions.explain: Since \(\Delta X=\lambda D/a\), increasing (a) decreases \(\Delta X\) (the fringes move closer together).

options: measuring the mass of the electron only
measuring the speed of light in vacuum

determining the wavelength of monochromatic light and proving the wave nature of light
questions.explain: Young's experiment is used to study interference, determine wavelength, determine the distance between fringes, and investigate the wave nature of light.

the separation between the slits is less than the wavelength of the incident light

summary.heading: 📋 Lesson Summary
items: Young's experiment produces two coherent sources by splitting the wavefront of a single light wave through two closely spaced slits.
The basic relation: \(\lambda=aX/nD\), and the fringe spacing \(\Delta X=\lambda D/a\).
Optical path difference \(\delta=a\sin\theta\): constructive interference at \(n\lambda\), destructive interference at \(\left(n+\tfrac12\right)\lambda\).
No fringes if the separation between the slits is less than the wavelength.
